name: Erik Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me your public line and the private thought behind it. What does a usual day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Erik, 43, and I lead the developers of pharmacy stock software at a tech company. I have a master’s degree and I’m good at finding why an expiry date or batch number was copied wrongly. I read overnight stock errors, trace the record and check a fix with a pharmacist before release. I use AI now and then to summarise long error logs after colleagues have tried it, but I still compare the batch label myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household relying on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Mila, runs a small upholstery workshop, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My developer pay is typical for a lead, and we have about three months of expenses saved. There are some similar jobs nearby. Mila’s orders vary, so the household budget uses the quiet month, not the busy one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau leaves people checking expiry dates before a pharmacy orders more stock. A short log summary helps, but a batch label needs a real check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my job to stay steady, though Mila’s workshop income moves around. Three months saved is enough for a small delay, not a long slump in orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking AI log summaries against batch labels and pharmacist notes. I’d move 170 monthly into savings only when Mila’s orders cover the workshop bills. In the first year I’d ask the team to keep a pharmacist sign-off on corrected expiry records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the workshop, calm about my own work. The mortgage is fine if both incomes hold near their usual level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expiry mistake made you cautious?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A batch once looked fresh on screen after someone copied the wrong year. A pharmacist showed me the printed batch label before we stopped a wrong reorder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend during a busy workshop month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Mila we can keep the old dining chairs until her quieter season ends. We do not need to spend the three-month reserve to prove the workshop is doing well.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking expiry records.
I would keep **pharmacist sign-off** on corrected batches.
think: I expect my **lead job** to remain steady.
I worry **workshop orders** could dip longer than our three-month cushion.
do: **Keep** comparing AI summaries with batch labels and pharmacist notes.
**Save** 170 monthly only when upholstery orders cover workshop bills.
**Keep** pharmacist sign-off and delay new dining chairs until the workshop’s quiet season ends.
feel: **Uneasy** about variable orders, with my developer pay secure.
S0.quote: A pharmacist showed me the printed batch label before we stopped a wrong reorder.
fieldNote: His **occasional AI use** remains tied to original printed batch labels and a pharmacist’s review of wrong-year stock.
Three months saved helps, but **seasonal upholstery orders** limit his monthly transfer.

steps.text: Keep checking pharmacy batch labels against AI summaries and pharmacist notes
Save 170 monthly only when upholstery orders cover workshop bills
Keep old dining chairs until upholstery workshop quiet season ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could draft stock code, order supplies and answer pharmacies faster. I would ask for a trial against old expiry mistakes before we shorten the review time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think our team might shrink if routine stock fixes move to software. Mila’s booking messages could also be automated, although the fabric work is still hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d run the approved assistant against fourteen old wrong-year records with a pharmacist. If it catches them all, I’d learn to review its corrections during paid work time. In the first year, if my hours fall, Mila and I would stop the planned workshop advertising unless paid orders show it earns more than it costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my hours and Mila’s uneven orders. A tool that finds a mistake is useful, but it may still change how many developers are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about pharmacist review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the copied-year case to my manager and ask who checks the printed label after the software proposes a fix. The pharmacist should not be rushed out of the review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really stop the workshop advertising?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare paid orders with the advertising cost before stopping it. If it pays for itself, we keep it even if my hours shrink.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed stock code, ordering and replies.
I would demand an **old-error trial** before shortening pharmacist review.
think: I fear **fewer developers** if routine stock fixes move to AI.
I expect **booking messages** to change before Mila’s hands-on upholstery.
do: **Test** an approved assistant against fourteen old wrong-year records.
**Learn** correction review during paid time only if all records pass.
**Pause** workshop advertising if my hours fall and paid orders fail to cover its cost.
feel: **Anxious** about code hours and uneven workshop income.
S1.quote: The pharmacist should not be rushed out of the review.
fieldNote: His **fourteen-case gate** and paid learning time precede any automated expiry changes.
The **advertising cut** requires both lost hours and evidence that paid orders fail to cover cost.

steps.text: Learn approved expiry review during paid time if fourteen old cases pass
Pause workshop advertising if developer hours fall and orders fail to cover cost

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches pharmacy-stock code in 2028. Hands-on robots arrive around 2031, so Mila’s upholstery may have more time than my desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect most stock-code roles could disappear, including mine. Three months saved will not carry a mortgage if upholstery orders also fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company for written severance and keep the proposed workshop machine deposit in cash. I’d check actual local openings rather than assume pharmacies will still hire coders. In the first year after 2028, if laid off, I’d apply for real vacancies and eligible income help while Mila keeps the current workshop orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I expect a large cut to my pay. A new upholstery machine cannot replace a developer wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the workshop machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Mila to wait on the new machine until we know both incomes. If her current equipment needs a safety repair, we still pay for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could family help during a job search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my father for two interview afternoons of childcare only if he is well enough. I would not ask him to draw down his own savings for our mortgage.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach stock code before upholstery robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues Mila’s **hands-on work** may change later.
think: I expect **stock-code jobs** could disappear, including mine.
Our **three-month reserve** cannot carry the mortgage if orders fall.
do: **Delay** workshop machine purchase, retain deposit for bills and fund safety repairs to current equipment.
**Request** written severance and check actual local openings now.
**Apply** for real jobs and eligible help if laid off, asking my father for childcare if well.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and a short cash runway.
S2.quote: A new upholstery machine cannot replace a developer wage.
fieldNote: His **2028 code exposure** precedes robots around 2031 that may reach hands-on upholstery.
His **father’s childcare** depends on health, while the machine waits and safety repairs remain funded.

steps.text: Delay new machine, hold deposit for mortgage and fund current equipment safety repairs
Apply for actual local jobs if laid off after 2028
Apply for eligible income help after layoff; ask father for interview childcare only if well

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to learn what pharmacists still need from stock records. Thinking AI reaches my code in 2031; hands-on robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect fewer developer roles, but two supervised stocktakes could show whether I can find batch mismatches. I cannot assume pharmacy stock audits stay paid after full thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask permission to join the pharmacy’s next two expiry stocktakes on paid company time and count batch mismatches with a pharmacist. If the company refuses, I’d use a free batch-control checklist on archived records. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d apply only for real stock-audit openings that pay enough for our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about code work, with time to test a different skill. I would keep the workshop machine money in cash until our future income is clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you prove stockroom skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring a count of the mismatched batches I found and ask the pharmacist to check my reasons. A tidy report would mean little if I missed an expired box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for certification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not buy an audit certificate just because the date is five years away. I would need a real vacancy requiring it and a cost our family can afford.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to learn real batch checks.
I know **2034 robots** follow the earlier stock-code change.
think: I expect **fewer developer roles**, even if the two supervised stocktakes show I can learn the audit.
I cannot assume **stock audits** stay paid work after full thinking AI reaches pharmacy records.
do: **Join** two expiry stocktakes only with pharmacy permission and paid company time.
**Practise** with a free batch-control checklist on archived records if refused.
**Apply** for real mortgage-paying stock-audit roles only if coding ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about code income, with time for a limited trial.
S3.quote: I cannot assume pharmacy stock audits stay paid after full thinking AI.
fieldNote: His **two-stocktake trial** produces a checked mismatch count instead of a speculative certificate.
The **pharmacy approval** and paid company time are conditions; archived records provide a free fallback.

steps.text: Join two stocktakes only with pharmacy permission and paid company time; otherwise use free checklist
Apply after 2031 coding loss for real stock-audit roles paying mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to improve stock records and teach apprentices. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036; hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my pay to hold for now, but workshop orders may still dip. I would not call three months of savings a permanent cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking batch corrections with pharmacists and save 170 monthly only when workshop orders cover bills. I’d help Mila’s new apprentice compare fabric dye-lot labels on one Saturday each quarter, without charging the workshop. In the first year after 2036, if coding work ends, I’d search real local openings before considering a family move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long term, with current developer pay secure. I can teach fabric dye-lot checks without spending the family reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the apprentice learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the apprentice two fabrics with similar colours but different dye-lot numbers. That is a better lesson than letting software fill every blank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mila and I would keep the current house unless a real job offer covers new housing and school travel. We would not move the children for a prediction.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to improve stock records.
I know **2039 robots** follow the earlier code change.
think: I expect my **developer pay** to hold for now.
I still watch **workshop orders** and a limited three-month reserve.
do: **Keep** checking pharmacy batches and save 170 monthly when workshop orders cover bills.
**Teach** the upholstery apprentice fabric dye-lot checks quarterly for free.
**Search local openings** after 2036 coding loss; move only for a real job offer covering new housing and school travel.
feel: **Uneasy** about later work, with my wage safe for now.
S4.quote: I can teach fabric dye-lot checks without spending the family reserve.
fieldNote: He connects **apprentice teaching** with fabric dye-lot checks while keeping household cash protected.
The **family move** requires a real job offer covering housing and school travel.

steps.text: Keep checking pharmacy batch corrections with pharmacists
Save 170 monthly only when workshop orders cover bills
Search real local openings if coding ends after 2036
Move children only for real job offer covering new housing and school travel

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my stock-code pay could stop before Mila’s upholstery changes. Written severance, paid time to learn batch checks and actual openings would help. My father could watch the children for interviews if his health allows, but he cannot become our income plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who notices a wrong expiry year when the pharmacy software says the box is fresh. A tidy stock screen cannot change the date printed on the medicine.

headlineQuote: A tidy stock screen cannot change the date printed on the medicine.
portrait: Erik is a **43-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree and strong skill in pharmacy stock code.
He uses **AI occasionally** for log summaries, checking them against printed batch labels and pharmacists’ notes.
His partner’s **upholstery workshop** has variable orders, while hands-on robots would follow thinking AI by about three years.
He tests **approved tools**, protects mortgage cash and seeks real stock jobs that pay enough for the family.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his code wage before upholstery work has time to change.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid batch-check learning and actual openings would help.
